A useful onboarding process can be both clear and human.

In April 2026, I ran an onboarding pilot at Northline Studio with 12 clients. We introduced a checklist of required files, and the median number of follow-up emails fell from 5 to 2. Clients could still contact the team directly, which mattered to me: a checklist should help a conversation along, not stand in for one.

The experience has me thinking about the small moments where a clear prompt can make it easier for people to take the next step. A list of required files gives clients something concrete to work from and gives the team a shared point of reference when questions come up. It is a modest tool, but it is also a useful invitation to examine the experience from the client’s perspective.

I would love feedback on the checklist. What makes a required-files list easy to use, and where have you seen one create more questions than it answers? I’m interested in the details that make guidance feel helpful while keeping the door open to a direct conversation.

— Jordan Lee
